source: Graviet, Shah (2026) Returning to Development States: When Full Sandbox Snapshots Help Coding Agents
finding: First equal-token test of a Go-Explore-style archive against independent retry. Archive of full sandbox snapshots, one root run plus up to two restored children, versus three fresh attempts. Retry won clearly. The authors expected the opposite and say the broad hypothesis is refuted on these tasks.
numbers: Claude Haiku 4.5, Terminal-Bench 2.0, 5 tasks x 5 seeds, 1M tokens per seed, pre-registered task set. Retry 17/25 (68%), snapshot branching 6/25 (24%). Per task retry vs branch: git-multibranch 5/5 vs 1/5, extract-elf 4/5 vs 3/5, custom-memory-heap-crash 3/5 vs 1/5, code-from-image 3/5 vs 1/5, large-scale-text-editing 2/5 vs 0/5.
quote: We initially hypothesized that branching from promising snapshots would solve more tasks than independent retry under a fixed token budget.
limits: One cheap model, 5 tasks picked for medium difficulty, file-centric tasks. Selector was a simple progress heuristic (file edits, test activity), not an LLM as in IGE, and there were no novelty-judging calls. Baseline was retry, not best-of-N judging or tree search (authors say so). Uniform budget split was not tuned. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is no longer empty and the one result is negative. An archive that costs tokens to build and to resume can lose to plain resampling at equal budget. Our archive arm must be compared with retry at equal total tokens, with root cost counted.

source: Graviet, Shah (2026) Returning to Development States (failure analysis and recovery runs)
finding: Why resuming lost. Four named failure modes: budget fragmentation (root and children share one budget; a weak root means a weak archive and short children run out), wrong-state attractors (faithful restore keeps a plausible but wrong implementation and the child edits around it), handoff cost (child gets the machine but not the parent's understanding), weak state selection (early selector ranked package installs and claimed completion as progress). Resuming still rescued some failed roots.
numbers: Four cases where the root failed and a restored child later passed (3 on extract-elf, 1 on custom-memory-heap-crash). Follow-up: children of failed roots recovered 67% of roots on extract-elf (independent retry overall 38% on that task) and 13% on regex-log. One inspected child used about 190,000 tokens over 26 steps; a successful fresh retry used about 90,000 over 11 steps.
limits: Recovery rates come from a separate follow-up; N not stated beyond task level. Single inspected trajectory for the handoff figure.
agent_relevance: Resume points should be chosen by a signal tied to the checker, not by activity. Pass a short state summary to the resumed run, or it re-pays the discovery cost. Count the root's tokens in the archive arm.

source: Graviet, Shah (2026) Returning to Development States (what state to save)
finding: The value of the saved state depends on where the progress lives. When progress is in files, a git diff or replayed commands is as good as a full snapshot. When progress is outside the files (a database), only the full state works.
numbers: extract-elf: children from git diff or replayed commands succeeded 4/4 seeds; full-snapshot children often ran out of budget. staged-service-repair (custom task, 200,000 remaining tokens, same planted checkpoint): clean restart 0/5, git diff only 0/5, full snapshot 4/5; snapshot runs solved with 21k to 41k tokens.
limits: staged-service-repair was built by the authors to need the database, so it shows a possible benefit, not a typical one. Five seeds. Not pooled with the headline.
agent_relevance: State key lesson for a reasoning agent: store the cheapest representation that carries the progress (plan, partial proof, working code), not the whole context. Progress that exists only in hidden reasoning cannot be restored; write it out.

source: Kim, Hwang (2025) Dual-Scale World Models for LLM Agents Towards Hard-Exploration Problems (GLoW), Table 1 and cost
finding: Independent re-implementation of IGE, ReAct, Reflexion and ICRL on 10 Jericho text games with GPT-4.1-mini at the same 1,000 environment steps. Per-run API cost was about the same for all LLM methods. IGE was not uniformly better than ReAct.
numbers: 3 seeds, mean max score. IGE vs ReAct: Zork1 44.3 vs 48.3, Deephome 71.3 vs 11.0, Detective 316.7 vs 113.3, Enchanter 50.0 vs 46.7, Ludicorp 28.3 vs 19.7, Pentari 30.0 vs 30.0, Ztuu 15.0 vs 18.7. Cost per 1,000-step run $4 to $6 for all methods, 'negligible differences' (gpt-4.1-mini at $0.40 / $1.60 per M tokens). GLoW beat IGE on 8 of 10 games.
limits: Equal steps and about equal dollars, but the dollar figure is a range, not a per-method table. Baselines were re-implemented by the GLoW authors with a valid-action soft constraint, so ReAct is stronger than in older reports. Jericho may be partly known to the model (contamination check: under 20% on navigation questions).
agent_relevance: Near-equal-cost evidence that an LLM-selected archive helps on games with long dead ends (Deephome, Detective) and does nothing or hurts on others (Zork1, Ztuu). Treat the archive as a tool for stuck states, not a default.

source: Kim, Hwang (2025) GLoW, ablation Table 2 (state selection)
finding: Choosing the resume state with an LLM that reads whole high-score trajectories beats choosing from the raw frontier, and beats IGE's per-state judgement on most games. Removing parts of GLoW falls back toward IGE.
numbers: Mean +- SE over 3 seeds. Zork1: full 73.0, state selection with W_global removed 62.0, trajectory frontier removed 61.7, all removed 51.3, standard IGE 44.3. Ludicorp: 73.7, 63.3, 63.3, 22.0, 28.3. Deephome: 75.0, 61.3, 57.7, 56.0, IGE 71.3 (IGE high here). Standard error often 10 to 26 points on Deephome and Ludicorp.
limits: 3 seeds and wide error bars. Differences on Deephome are inside noise. Every GLoW component is LLM-based, so this does not compare model selection with a code rule.
agent_relevance: Model-based selection with global context beats model-based selection on single states. It does not tell us whether a count or score rule would match it (gap 4 stays open).

source: Kim, Hwang (2025) GLoW, Table 3 (explorations per selected state)
finding: Direct data on how much exploration to do after resuming. With a fixed 1,000-step budget and 50-step bursts, 3 bursts per selected state gave the best scores. One burst per selection (frequent re-selection) and 5 bursts both did worse.
limits: 3 seeds, SE up to 26 on Deephome. Part of the effect of n is the multi-path reflection step (n=1 turns it off), so burst count and reflection are mixed. No comparison with restarting from the root at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: A resume should be a few short bursts (about 3) before the next selection, not one burst and not a long commitment. A usable default for our archive operator, to be re-tuned on our tasks.

source: El, Yuksekgonul, Zou (2025) Inefficiencies of Meta Agents for Agent Design
finding: Ablation of what the generator sees from the archive in ADAS-style agent search (MGSM, DROP, MMLU, GPQA, 3 runs). Showing the generator all earlier agents did not beat showing it only the seed library. Showing only the top 7 by score did better, but made the agents more alike.
numbers: Average best-agent score on the training split: cumulative 55.0, parallel (ignore prior designs) 60.0, evolutionary (top 7 by score) 60.3. MGSM best agent: cumulative 41.4, parallel 56.2, evolutionary 56.5. Parallel gave the highest coverage and the most diverse agents. Designed agents also cost more per query than seed agents; break-even only at about 15,000 test examples on DROP and MMLU.
limits: Agent design with a model as designer, not state resumption. Three runs. Held-out gains are smaller and noisy (test columns differ from train).
agent_relevance: Feeding the model the whole archive is not free: it can hurt. Give the generator a curated top-k, or none, and keep a path with no archive context for diversity. Consistent with G8 and with the bloat concern.

source: Lange, Imajuku, Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended and Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
finding: Ablations on circle packing in an LLM program-evolution archive. Parent choice by fitness plus a few-children weight beat hill climbing and a no-history baseline. A cheap code-embedding similarity filter (reject above 0.95) gave large gains over no filter. Adding an LLM novelty judge on top gave only a marginal gain.
numbers: Archive size 10 to 50 programs across tasks (circle packing 40), 2 to 4 islands, novelty threshold 0.95 on code embeddings. New best circle packing with 150 samples. Weighted parent sampling 'consistently outperforms both random search and hill climbing' on all tasks; hill climbing 'plateaus quickly'. Exact ablation scores are in figures only and were not read as numbers.
quote: embedding-based rejection sampling provides substantial performance gains over no rejection sampling
limits: Effect sizes described in text, not read from a table. Single task for the filter ablation. Task has a numeric fitness checker, unlike open reasoning. Authors are also the system's authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: for code-like entries, an embedding-distance rule plus fitness and few-children weighting does most of what a model judge does. A model judge is a luxury; try code dedupe first. Same weighting idea as DGM.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Huxley-Godel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine
finding: A parent's own benchmark score is a weak predictor of how good its descendants will be. Selecting by the scores of the whole descendant line (clade), sampled with Thompson sampling, predicted descendants better and used fewer compute hours than DGM and SICA.
numbers: Pearson correlation of selection score with true clade productivity, weighted: SWE-Verified-60: SICA 0.444, DGM 0.285, HGM 0.778; Polyglot: SICA 0.274, DGM 0.383, HGM 0.626. Best agent after 800 evaluations: SWE-Verified-60 SICA 50.0, DGM 53.3, HGM 56.7 (start 40); Polyglot 25.4, 27.1, 30.5 (start 20.3). CPU hours: DGM 1231 vs HGM 517 on SWE-Verified-60; DGM 2385 vs HGM 347 on Polyglot.
limits: Agent-code archive, not reasoning states. Cheaper backbone than the DGM paper, so numbers are not comparable to DGM's original. Single run per method as far as the text states. One typo in the text (0.8783 vs 0.873 in the table).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: it is not just an anecdote that low scorers seed good lineages. The score of an entry is a weak guide to its use as a resume point (r about 0.3 to 0.4). Rank resume points by what happened after earlier resumes from them (children count and child scores), not by own score.

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2025/2026) Darwin Godel Machine (re-opened for selection rule and dips)
finding: The resume point is chosen by a fixed code formula, not by the model: sigmoid of score times 1/(1+functioning children). Every non-perfect agent keeps a non-zero chance. Greedy best-only selection is worse. The two dips in the lineage of the best agent are shown in a figure and described in the text.
numbers: Weight = sigmoid(10*(score - 0.5)) * 1/(1+children); k=2 parents per iteration on SWE-bench, k=4 on Polyglot. Greedy ablation: SWE-bench 39.7 vs 50.0 (DGM), Polyglot 30.0 vs 38.0. Lineage of the best agent has 'two performance dips'; at iterations 4 and 56 a child scored below its parent and the path later led to an agent above all predecessors.
limits: One run per arm (about 22,000 USD for a SWE-bench run), no variance. The dips are two events in one lineage, not a count over many runs. Objective-hacking case study in the appendix.
agent_relevance: G8 is met by construction: the selector is code, the generator is the model. Gap 8 stays open as a controlled count. The formula is a ready design for our resume operator.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS)
finding: On a checker task (ARC-AGI as program synthesis, scored on the example grids) a tree that refines earlier answers did not beat plain repeated sampling at 128 model calls. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContest, adaptive wider-or-deeper search beat repeated sampling slightly. At larger budgets on ARC the tree overtook sampling.
numbers: Budget 2^7 = 128 API calls, 100 public ARC-AGI evaluation problems, Pass@2. GPT-4o: repeated sampling 15.0, AB-MCTS-A (Beta) 14.0, AB-MCTS-M 12.3, standard MCTS 9.0, sequential refinement 8.7. DeepSeek-V3: 18.6 repeated sampling vs 18.3 AB-MCTS-A (Gaussian) vs 14.0 MCTS vs 10.0 refinement. CodeContest GPT-4o: sampling 37.9, AB-MCTS-M 40.6. DeepSeek-V3 on ARC up to 512 calls: AB-MCTS 'continues to improve substantially' from 200 to 500 while repeated sampling plateaus (figure only).
limits: Budget is API calls, not tokens; refinement calls carry longer prompts, so token-equal sampling would look better still. 2024 non-reasoning models. Run-to-run spread (3 to 5 runs) is as large as several gaps.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: on ARC with a checker, wide sampling is the strong baseline at small budgets and tree refinement pays only later. Our archive arm needs a repeated-sampling control at equal calls and tokens, and should switch from wide to deep after cheap breadth is spent.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Evolving Deeper LLM Thinking (Mind Evolution)
finding: Population search with islands, LLM crossover and a critic-author refine step, guided by an automatic evaluator, beat best-of-N and sequential revision, with cost reported per instance. It needs a checker. Best-of-N was the second best on Trip Planning.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash. TravelPlanner val: 1-pass 5.6%, best-of-N 55.6% ($0.47 per instance, 472 calls), sequential revision+ 82.8% ($2.75), Mind Evolution 95.6% ($0.29, 174 calls); with Pro on unsolved: 100% val, 99.9% test. Trip Planning val: best-of-N 77.2% ($0.10), sequential revision 74.4%, Mind Evolution 96.2% ($0.17). Meeting Planning val: best-of-N 69.4% ($0.39), Mind Evolution 85.0% ($0.52), +Pro 98.4% ($2.55).
limits: Cost is averaged per instance and search stops when solved, so arms do not spend the same budget. Population search, not an archive of resumable states. Natural-language planning with an exact checker. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: a checker-driven population loop can be cheaper per instance than best-of-N (TravelPlanner) or somewhat dearer (Meeting Planning), with +15 to +40 points. Strongest evidence so far that checker-guided archives work on reasoning-like tasks, but it is population search and not matched in tokens.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2026) Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis (SOAR), ARC-AGI
finding: On ARC-AGI program synthesis, the same 6,000 candidates solve more tasks when half are refinements of earlier programs than when all are fresh samples. Search alone saturates (about 5.2k attempts for the 7B model). Solution diversity falls across iterations for solved tasks. Programs that hard-code outputs pass the examples but are brittle.
numbers: ARC-test % solved, Sample-6k vs Sample&Refine-6k: Qwen2.5-Coder 7B 5.63 vs 14.25, 14B 12.63 vs 19.87, 32B 12.88 vs 25.25, 72B 18.50 vs 25.62, Mistral-Large-2 19.75 vs 26.25. One-shot: GPT-4.1 8.00, Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75, o3-mini 38.25. Majority vote groups programs by their test output grid.
limits: Counts candidates (calls), not tokens; refinement prompts are longer. The learned part (fine-tuning) is out of scope for a scaffold. No closed model was run with search. The hard-coding point is in an appendix, with no rate given.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: positive for checker + refine at equal candidate count. Gap 3: grouping by output grid (a behaviour key) is a working state key for programs. Gap 10: check answers on inputs the program was not built from, and filter programs that copy training outputs.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) rises about log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude. With an automatic verifier this becomes accuracy; with majority vote or reward models the gain stops after a few hundred samples. So breadth does not saturate at 20 on checkable tasks, and the selector decides what you keep.
numbers: CodeContests with Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples) vs single-sample SOTA 43%. MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% (100 samples) to 98.44% (10,000), but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Independent runs from scratch, no archive. Coverage with an oracle verifier is an upper bound. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the N=20 saturation seen in red-teaming (K16) counts distinct attack types, not solved problems; on checkable tasks more samples keep helping. Keep a wide sampling arm in the budget. Also supports G8: the picker must be a real verifier, not a vote or a model score.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) First Return, Entropy-Eliciting Explore (FR3E)
finding: Go-Explore-style return inside one math reasoning trace: cut the trace at high-entropy tokens, restart rollouts from each cut prefix, use outcomes as value signals. This is RL training (GRPO), not a scaffold, but it is a measured test of 'return to a mid-reasoning state and branch' on math with a checker.
numbers: Accuracy FR3E vs GRPO++ on three Qwen2.5 bases. AIME24: Math-7B 39.1 vs 39.1, 7B 25.2 vs 22.7, 32B 40.2 vs 34.1. Average over 8 benchmarks: 60.3 vs 58.5, 57.3 vs 54.3, 65.6 vs 62.5 (+1.8, +3.0, +3.1). The math-specialised 7B gained nothing on AIME24. Authors say matching group size is impossible and inference cost differs.
limits: Training method; gains may come from better credit assignment, not from the return itself. Cost not matched. AIME24 is avg@32.
agent_relevance: Weak positive: returning to uncertain prefixes helps a little where the model is not already specialised. Suggests the resume point for a reasoning archive could be a high-uncertainty step in the chain, but this was not tested as a scaffold.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement
finding: Model-valued tree search over partial software fixes. The model's value estimate picked the correct final solution 73% of the time; a separate debate-style discriminator raised that to 84%. The search gave a 23% mean relative gain over the same agent without search.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite resolve rate, SWE-Search vs Moatless-Adapted: GPT-4o 31.0 vs 25.7, GPT-4o-mini 17.0 vs 13.0, Qwen-2.5-72B 24.7 vs 18.0, DeepSeek-V2.5 21.0 vs 16.3, Llama-3.1-70B 17.7 vs 13.6; mean +23% relative. Max 100 iterations, 3 expansions per node. A compute-matched table (Pass@5 in one run vs 5 runs) was garbled in extraction and not used.
limits: Value function and generator are the same model family, so the 73% is a self-judge number. Relative gain is smallest for the strongest model (+17% GPT-4o vs +22 to +27% for the other four). Not a Go-Explore archive.
agent_relevance: G8 support: a separate final selector beat the search's own value. Gap 7 hint: relative gain was smaller for the strongest model, but five models and one run each cannot separate that from noise.

source: Gandhi, Neubig (2026) Go-Browse: Training Web Agents with Structured Exploration (re-opened)
finding: Archive key is the URL, a natural key the web gives for free. Resuming from the stored page (prefixed sampling) succeeds more than starting from the home page, most for deeper pages and weaker models. Returning to many stored pages widens coverage at equal task count. A cheap feasibility filter cut wasted steps.
numbers: Resets to discovered pages vs unique URLs visited, 30 tasks per domain fixed: 1 reset 183, 5 resets 214, 15 resets 260. FeasibilityChecker removed 403 tasks = 3.2K rollouts (about 29.4K steps), 13% fewer steps for the same positive data. Share of successful trajectories by solver: Qwen-2.5-7B 29.5%, GPT-4o-mini 36.6%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 33.9%. Fine-tuned 7B reaches 21.7% on WebArena (+2.4 over GPT-4o-mini).
limits: Output is training data, not a test-time scaffold. The prefixed-vs-unprefixed result is in a figure (success vs node depth), no table. WebArena is a restorable simulator.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: where the task gives a natural discrete key (URL, file, test id), use it. Gap 6: returning to a stored state beats re-deriving it, more for weaker models (supports K10). Gap 10: a cheap feasibility check before spending rollouts saves about 13%.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2026) SOAR, search gain by model size (Table 1 re-read from PDF raw text)
finding: The gain from refinement search is not smaller for bigger open models in this range. Absolute gain over plain sampling at equal candidate count stays roughly 6 to 12 points from 7B to a 123B model. The strong closed models were run one-shot only, so the question for current frontier models remains unmeasured.
numbers: Sample&Refine-6k minus Sample-6k (ARC-test points): 7B +8.6, 14B +7.2, 32B +12.4, 72B +7.1, Mistral-Large-2 +6.5. One-shot Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75, GPT-4.1 8.00, o3-mini 38.25; the 14B model with learned SOAR search reached 42.75.
limits: Layout-mode text extraction misaligned table rows; values were taken from raw-mode extraction and checked against the prose (7B 14.25, 14B 19.87). Open models only; no search run on current frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: partial. No sign that the search gain shrinks across 7B to 123B, but nothing is measured at the current frontier. Re-measure our arm at two model strengths before trusting K10.
